name: Network Security
description: Security of network protocols and infrastructure: routing, DNS, BGP, middleboxes, DDoS, and traffic analysis.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list (all USENIX Security 2018) show network security split across several long-standing fronts. One thread targets the abuse of core Internet naming and trust infrastructure: FANCI: Feature-based Automated NXDomain Classification and Intelligence (2018) mined non-existent-domain responses to flag DGA malware, while Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP (2018) showed that BGP route hijacks could subvert the web PKI by fooling domain-validation checks. A second thread is measurement and circumvention: End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks (2018) audited how poorly providers authenticate senders, and Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship (2018) extended remote censorship measurement beyond DNS/IP blocking. A third thread is anonymity and traffic confidentiality, with NetHide: Secure and Practical Network Topology Obfuscation (2018) hiding topology from traceroute and several Tor-focused papers on performance and covert channels.

Around 2019-2020 the work shifted toward the network's own control and data planes as attack surface. The CrossPath Attack (USENIX 2019) weaponized shared links to disrupt the SDN control channel, and EPIC (USENIX 2020) pushed path-aware architectures where every packet is verified in the data plane. Protocol-implementation security also matured from ad hoc testing into systematic state exploration, exemplified by Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing (USENIX 2020), with Composition Kills (USENIX 2020) showing that combining correctly-specified email components still breaks sender authentication.

The early 2020s brought two big breakthroughs. First, programmable switches turned line-rate hardware into a defense platform: Jaqen (USENIX 2021) delivered switch-native volumetric DDoS detection and mitigation, Ripple (USENIX 2021) built a decentralized link-flooding defense, and An Efficient Design of Intelligent Network Data Plane (USENIX 2023) put ML models directly in the data plane. Meanwhile attackers found new amplification vectors, most strikingly in Weaponizing Middleboxes for TCP Reflected Amplification (USENIX 2021), which broke the assumption that reflection attacks needed UDP. Protocol fuzzing also generalized, from Stateful Greybox Fuzzing (USENIX 2022) to packet-sequence-oriented Bleem (USENIX 2023).

The most active recent frontier is the arms race over encrypted-traffic analysis and its defenses, increasingly driven by deep learning. Website fingerprinting moved into realistic settings with Online Website Fingerprinting (USENIX 2022) and was sharpened by robust traffic representations in Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation (USENIX 2023), while Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations (USENIX 2021) and Rosetta (USENIX 2023) attacked and hardened DL classifiers from opposite sides. Censorship research likewise turned to the protocols themselves, as How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic (USENIX 2023) reverse-engineered nation-state filtering of fully encrypted flows. Network security today thus sits at the intersection of programmable infrastructure, ML-based analysis, and the adversarial robustness of both.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats network security as a defense-and-measurement problem tackled one protocol at a time. On the defensive side, Kitsune: An Ensemble of Autoencoders for Online Network Intrusion Detection (NDSS 2018) showed that lightweight unsupervised autoencoders could flag intrusions online, kicking off a long ML-for-traffic thread that runs through the whole decade. Alongside it sat a cluster of protocol-specific attack papers: Automated Attack Discovery in TCP Congestion Control Using a Model-guided Approach (NDSS 2018) used model-guided search to surface congestion-control exploits, Exposing Congestion Attack on Emerging Connected Vehicle based Traffic Signal Control (NDSS 2018) broke a real traffic-control deployment, and Preventing (Network) Time Travel with Chronos (NDSS 2018) hardened NTP against time-shifting adversaries. The infrastructure-and-measurement instinct was already present too, with Cloud Strife: Mitigating the Security Risks of Domain-Validated Certificates (NDSS 2018) and A Large-scale Analysis of Content Modification by Open HTTP Proxies (NDSS 2018) auditing the trust and middlebox plumbing of the web.

Around 2019-2020 two shifts stand out. First, traffic analysis matured from a niche Tor concern — Inside Job: Applying Traffic Analysis to Measure Tor from Within (NDSS 2018) — into a broad privacy threat: FlowPrint: Semi-Supervised Mobile-App Fingerprinting on Encrypted Network Traffic (NDSS 2020), Packet-Level Signatures for Smart Home Devices (NDSS 2020), and Practical Traffic Analysis Attacks on Secure Messaging Applications (NDSS 2020) all showed that encryption alone leaks which app, device, or contact you are using, prompting defenses like Statistical Privacy for Streaming Traffic (NDSS 2019). Second, censorship and evasion became a running battle, with The use of TLS in Censorship Circumvention (NDSS 2019), Measuring the Deployment of Network Censorship Filters at Global Scale (NDSS 2020), SymTCP: Eluding Stateful Deep Packet Inspection with Automated Discrepancy Discovery (NDSS 2020), and Detecting Probe-resistant Proxies (NDSS 2020) mapping the cat-and-mouse between inspectors and circumventors. This period also pushed defense into hardware, as Poseidon: Mitigating Volumetric DDoS Attacks with Programmable Switches (NDSS 2020) moved DDoS mitigation onto the data plane.

The early-2020s consolidated those threads. Programmable switches became a platform rather than a one-off trick — FlowLens: Enabling Efficient Flow Classification for ML-based Network Security Applications (NDSS 2021) fused in-network telemetry with machine learning — while automated reasoning about protocols matured through NetPlier: Probabilistic Network Protocol Reverse Engineering from Message Traces (NDSS 2021). Attacks kept climbing the stack and into new infrastructure: IMP4GT: IMPersonation Attacks in 4G NeTworks (NDSS 2020) hit cellular authentication, ROV++: Improved Deployable Defense against BGP Hijacking (NDSS 2021) tackled interdomain routing, PMTUD is not Panacea: Revisiting IP Fragmentation Attacks against TCP (NDSS 2022) revived a supposedly-dead TCP threat, and Partitioning Ethereum without Eclipsing It (NDSS 2023) extended eclipse-style partitioning to blockchain peer-to-peer networks. Detection meanwhile grew more structural, moving from flat features to graph reasoning in Euler: Detecting Network Lateral Movement via Scalable Temporal Graph Link Prediction (NDSS 2022) and Detecting Unknown Encrypted Malicious Traffic in Real Time via Flow Interaction Graph Analysis (NDSS 2023).

By 2024-2026 two forces dominate the frontier: large language models and the messy realities of Internet-scale infrastructure. Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing (NDSS 2024) used LLMs to fuzz protocol implementations without a formal spec, and 5G-Spector: An O-RAN Compliant Layer-3 Cellular Attack Detection Service (NDSS 2024) folded attack detection into standardized cellular architectures. The newest 2026 cohort reads as a return to core Internet hygiene, now studied with far richer data. Routing and time infrastructure are revisited under partial-deployment realism in Understanding the Stealthy BGP Hijacking Risk in the ROV Era and On Borrowed Time: Measurement-Informed Understanding of the NTP Pool's Robustness to Monopoly Attacks; spoofing and proxy abuse get fresh measurement in Aliens Among Us: Observing Private or Reserved IPs on the Public Internet and Beyond RTT: An Adversarially Robust Two-Tiered Approach For Residential Proxy Detection; and the field is openly wrestling with adversarial robustness of its own tools, as Strategic Games and Zero Shot Attacks on Heavy-Hitter Network Flow Monitoring shows that even line-rate DDoS monitors can be gamed. The through-line from 2018 to 2026 is clear: the community keeps building smarter detectors and in-network defenses, while attackers keep exploiting the gap between how protocols are specified and how they are actually deployed.

sp.narrative:
The earliest S&P papers in this set treat network security as a set of distinct infrastructure problems, each attacked head-on. On the theory side, "Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two" (S&P 2018) proved a fundamental limit that still frames anonymous-communication design, while "Routing Around Congestion" (S&P 2018) showed that BGP could be turned into a live DDoS-mitigation tool. Alongside these ran a strong measurement thread on the certificate ecosystem — "Tracking Certificate Misissuance in the Wild" (S&P 2018) and, a year later, "Does Certificate Transparency Break the Web?" (S&P 2019) — quantifying how the Web's trust infrastructure actually behaves in practice rather than in principle.

Around 2019-2020 the focus widened from wired Internet plumbing to the messy edges: the radio, the physical medium, and abused infrastructure. "Breaking LTE on Layer Two" (S&P 2019) exposed cellular-layer attacks, "A Tale of Sea and Sky" (S&P 2020) broke maritime VSAT links, and "Resident Evil: Understanding Residential IP Proxy as a Dark Service" (S&P 2019) mapped how residential proxies launder malicious traffic. Meanwhile routing and DDoS work grew more adversarial and more infrastructural — "A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network" (S&P 2020) weaponized AS-level routing against a P2P network, and "On the Feasibility of Rerouting-Based DDoS Defenses" (S&P 2019) stress-tested the rerouting idea that Nyx had introduced. Censorship measurement also matured into standing infrastructure with "ICLab" (S&P 2020).

The 2020s brought two clear pivots. First, traffic analysis became a machine-learning arms race: "High Precision Open-World Website Fingerprinting" (S&P 2020) raised attack accuracy, "DeepCoFFEA" (S&P 2022) used metric learning to strengthen flow correlation against Tor, and "Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild" (S&P 2023) pushed attacks toward realistic browsing — answered by defenses like "Surakav" (S&P 2022) and the sobering "SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (S&P 2023). Second, protocols began to be handled formally and post-quantum: "Post-quantum WireGuard" (S&P 2021), the verified "IETF QUIC Record Layer" implementation (S&P 2021), and "Automated Attack Synthesis by Extracting Finite State Machines from Protocol Specification Documents" (S&P 2022), which mined specs to synthesize attacks automatically.

The most recent work shows the field consolidating around learned models of traffic and around securing the routing control plane. "TrafficFormer" (S&P 2025) brings pre-trained foundation-model techniques to traffic data, while "SoK: Decoding the Enigma of Encrypted Network Traffic Classifiers" (S&P 2025) takes stock of the whole classifier landscape under TLS 1.3. The 2026 cohort reads like a return to core infrastructure with sharper tools: "The Fault in Our Drafts" and "The Threat Landscape of IP Leasing in the RPKI Era" scrutinize RPKI's specification and its economics, "One Char to Rule Them All" systematically hunts silent DNS resolution bugs, "NetPanic" reopens the Linux kernel network stack as a remote attack surface, and "STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness" dismantles the telephone anti-spoofing standard. Reproducible testing ("Fizzle: A Framework for Deterministic and Reproducible Network Fuzzing") and revisited PQ designs ("Revisiting PQ Wireguard") round out a moment where the field is both automating attack discovery and re-auditing the infrastructure it thought it had secured.

ccs.narrative:
Network security research at CCS spans traffic analysis, protocol security, and infrastructure measurement. Deep learning transformed the field's attack capabilities beginning in 2018: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (CCS 2018) achieved near-perfect Tor traffic classification, and DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning (CCS 2018) correlated flows across the Tor network to deanonymize users. HoMonit: Monitoring Smart Home Apps from Encrypted Traffic (CCS 2018) extended traffic analysis to the IoT domain.

Protocol security in cellular networks became a distinct sub-community: A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) formally verified 5G AKA, and 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol (CCS 2019) uncovered new attacks across protocol layers. Let's Encrypt: An Automated Certificate Authority to Encrypt the Entire Web (CCS 2019) documented the PKI intervention that dramatically increased encrypted network traffic.

By 2021-2022, the community began critically examining ML-based network defenses. Realtime Robust Malicious Traffic Detection via Frequency Domain Analysis (CCS 2021) introduced frequency features resistant to evasion, while AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes (CCS 2022) challenged overconfident claims about ML detectors. Website fingerprinting research continued with transformer architectures in Transformer-based Model for Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attack (CCS 2023).

milestones.title: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
milestones.note: Showed deep CNNs break the best Tor fingerprinting defenses of 2018 with high accuracy.

milestones.title: DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning
milestones.note: Used deep learning to correlate Tor entry and exit flows, reliably deanonymizing users.

milestones.title: A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication
milestones.note: First rigorous formal analysis of the 5G AKA protocol identifying security gaps before large-scale rollout.

milestones.title: 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol
milestones.note: Uncovered cross-layer security and privacy attacks in 5G using property-directed formal reasoning.

milestones.title: Let's Encrypt: An Automated Certificate Authority to Encrypt the Entire Web
milestones.note: Documented how free automated certificates shifted the web from HTTP to HTTPS at scale.

milestones.title: TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting
milestones.note: Proposed traffic splitting across Tor entry guards as a practical defense against fingerprinting.

milestones.title: Realtime Robust Malicious Traffic Detection via Frequency Domain Analysis
milestones.note: Introduced frequency-domain features for traffic classification that are robust to adversarial evasion.

milestones.title: AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes
milestones.note: Critically audited ML-based network security detectors, exposing reliability and generalization failures.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, clustered in 2018, is dominated by a single force: deep learning arriving in network security. On the defensive side, "Kitsune: An Ensemble of Autoencoders for Online Network Intrusion Detection" (NDSS 2018) showed that unsupervised neural networks could flag intrusions at line rate, while "FANCI: Feature-based Automated NXDomain Classification and Intelligence" (USENIX 2018) attacked DGA malware through DNS. On the offensive side, the same techniques were turned against privacy: "Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning" (CCS 2018) and "DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning" (CCS 2018) used CNNs to shred Tor's protections. Alongside this empirical rush, "Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two" (S&P 2018) supplied the theoretical bedrock, proving that no anonymity system can have everything at once.

Two threads then pulled the field in new directions. First, protocol security got formal and adversarial: "Breaking LTE on Layer Two" (S&P 2019) and "5GReasoner" (CCS 2019) probed cellular standards, while "Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing" (USENIX 2020) and later "Stateful Greybox Fuzzing" (USENIX 2022) matured the fuzzing of stateful implementations. Second, defense moved into hardware: "Poseidon: Mitigating Volumetric DDoS Attacks with Programmable Switches" (NDSS 2020), "Jaqen" (USENIX 2021), "Ripple" (USENIX 2021), and "FlowLens" (NDSS 2021) all exploited programmable data planes to do detection and mitigation at wire speed rather than in software.

By the early 2020s the website-fingerprinting and traffic-analysis arms race had become self-reflective. Attacks kept escalating — "Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation" (USENIX 2023) and real-world evaluations like "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022) — even as defenses like "TrafficSliver" (CCS 2020) and adversarial perturbations ("Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time", USENIX 2021) fought back. But the mood shifted with "AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes" (CCS 2022) and "New Directions in Automated Traffic Analysis" (CCS 2021), which questioned whether the reported gains were real or artifacts of flawed evaluation, pushing the community toward more honest benchmarking and interpretability ("DeepAID", CCS 2021).

The most recent work splits along two lines. LLMs have entered protocol security, with "Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing" (NDSS 2024) using language models to test implementations that lack machine-readable specs. And the NDSS 2026 cohort marks a striking return to core Internet infrastructure and measurement: "Understanding the Stealthy BGP Hijacking Risk in the ROV Era" reveals that partial Route Origin Validation deployment creates new hijacking openings, "On Borrowed Time" measures the NTP Pool's fragility to monopoly attacks, "Aliens Among Us" tracks spoofed and reserved IPs in the wild, and "Beyond RTT" tackles residential proxy detection. After a decade dominated by machine learning on encrypted flows, the frontier has swung back toward the routing, naming, and timing substrates the whole network depends on — now studied with the measurement rigor the ML critiques demanded.
